The trade portion itself is a benefit to everyone by making products cheaper and more easily accessible to all parties while offering some sanctioned tariffs to protect local industries.

The issues come from the Arbitration council that will supposedly have more control than a sovereign nation and opens up a lot of doors for corruption. There are other, seemingly non trade and other unrelated issues in the agreement that probably don't belong there.

Reality is that the Arbitration is likely going to be used in cases of countries not following agreed upon labor standards, prohibitive tariffs, and the most controversial, laws that could impact trade in specific sectors by giving some companies exceptions to those laws. We don't know how this will actually work yet and it just has potential to be abused. Being made up of humans, it'll be abused in some way just as ever other piece of law is.

The TPP needs to be ratified by 85% of the trading partners. Japan or the US could choose not to and it would kill it on the spot. A few smaller nations could decide not to and make up more than 15%. Japan will ratify to solidify themselves as a better option than China (which refuses to enter into agreements that would force them to improve labor standards among other things). The US will probably ratify because they represent the most trading power and its what politicians want. It is a net benefit for everyone, but the potential for abuse is there and that's one of the problems.

... China refuses to enter into agreements that would force them to improve labor standards among other things ...

I think you've missed the entire point of the TPP. A major unstated goal of the TPP is an economic attack on China. Malaysia is a signatory to the TPP for fuck's sake. If you're not familiar with the country - they are one of the single biggest players in modern day slavery and human trafficking. Here is our report on them from 2014 where we gave them the lowest possible ratings in the world in terms of slave labor and human trafficking. Then in 2015 we magically decided to change them from being a key destination and source of human trafficking and slavery to simply being a potential source of concern. There was no improvement demonstrated from the country whatsoever with a number of reports indicating conditions have, if anything, deteriorated. The one and only reason we decided to start pretending they're not engaged in slave labor and human trafficking is so they could sign onto the TPP which has a clause prohibiting countries engaging in slavery from participating. This is no secret or 'conspiracy' either. Here, for instance, is a report from Reuters reporting on just as much. The TPP is corruption incarnate. China had no choice to join as China was not invited.

The major issue with arbitration is that companies will, more than ever, be able to sue for any action of a country that interferes with their "expected future profits." In other words it creates a legally bound entitlement to money for corporations. Phillip Morris, who is party to similar regional trade agreements, for instance, has used similar clauses to sue the governments of a wide array of nations for doing terrible things like requiring warnings about the health risks of smoking on cigarette labels. A legal entitlement to profit is the most absurd form of corporate welfare to date. Not only that but it gives corporations carte blanche to challenge our laws outside of our legal system. How ridiculous is that? Let's not even get into who the rotating 'judges' will be on these tribunals.

The only reasonable response here is that "Well NAFTA has similar ISDS clauses, and things haven't gone completely crazy yet." Pertinent article. I actually like the TPP. The reason for that is that I think things are still going to have to get quite a bit worse before they can get better, and the TPP is a great pill to help push that deterioration and cronyism along.
